target.title: Can We Read Speech Beyond the Lips? Rethinking RoI Selection for Deep Visual Speech Recognition
target.venue: arXiv preprint (no other venue stated on the first page)

entries.text: The authors frame systematic evaluation of extraoral facial regions as an overlooked RoI-selection problem in VSR.
entries.condition: Comparative study of mouth, whole-face, upper-face, and cheek inputs on word- and sentence-level VSR benchmarks.
entries.quote: However, this convention of explicit mouth RoI cropping inevitably brings about many questions.

entries.text: The authors claim extraoral facial information, including the upper face, consistently benefits VSR across varied data.
entries.condition: Authors' summary across the word-level LRW/LRW-1000 and sentence-level GRID experiments.

entries.text: The proposed face-based Cutout augmentation is intended to make the model learn discriminative cues across facial regions.
entries.condition: Randomly zero a spatial patch at the same position in every video frame during training.
entries.quote: During training, a patch within the face region is randomly zeroed.

entries.text: The authors claim their Cutout-plus-face model reaches state-of-the-art performance on all three benchmarks.
entries.condition: LRW and LRW-1000 word accuracy; GRID sentence WER/CER; see individual results and decoding conditions below.
entries.quote: enabling state-of-the-art performance on all three

entries.condition: LRW official train/validation/test partition; 500-class English word recognition.

entries.text: Word-level experiments use a 3D-ResNet18 backbone and a two-layer bidirectional GRU with 1,024 hidden units.
entries.condition: Word-level LRW and LRW-1000 classification experiments.

entries.text: Sentence-level experiments use LipNet, with temporal augmentation and dropout as recommended by its authors.
entries.condition: GRID sentence-level VSR.

entries.text: Faces are detected and landmarked with SeetaFace2, similarity-aligned using upper-face landmarks, and landmark tracks are smoothed with a temporal Gaussian kernel of width 3.
entries.condition: Preprocessing for all datasets; similarity transform and upper-face landmarks.
entries.quote: which are smoothed using a temporal Gaussian kernel of width 3.

entries.text: LRW and LRW-1000 faces are resized to 122×122 then randomly cropped to 112×112 in training; GRID faces are resized to 100×100.
entries.condition: Input preprocessing by dataset; GRID uses no random crop during training.

entries.text: Training uses random horizontal flips; word-level models use random crops and testing uses a central crop.
entries.condition: LRW/LRW-1000 and GRID training augmentation and test-time crop policy; GRID has no random crop.

entries.text: Cutout masks an identical spatial position across all frames of a training video.
entries.condition: Face-based training augmentation; patch position is fixed over time within a video.

entries.text: All models use Adam with default hyperparameters.
entries.condition: All word- and sentence-level VSR experiments.

entries.text: Word-level learning rates start at 0.0003 for stages I/II and 0.001 for stage III, then decay logarithmically from epoch 5 or 10 depending on Cutout.

entries.text: Sentence-level training uses learning rate 0.0001 and no weight decay.
entries.condition: GRID sentence-level VSR.

entries.text: The authors suggest face inputs may ease frontend transfer and connect VSR with broader face and speech-related vision tasks.

questions.q: Does the paper find that facial regions beyond the mouth help visual speech recognition?
questions.answer: Yes. The authors report useful information in the upper face and cheeks, with whole-face inputs improving LRW-1000 and GRID over mouth inputs; aligned faces are slightly worse on LRW, which they attribute probably to reduced mouth resolution. See t2, t26–t30, t33–t49, and t65.

questions.q: What is the main method contribution and how does Cutout perform?
questions.answer: The method applies temporally consistent Cutout masks to aligned face videos to encourage use of extraoral cues. It gives 85.02% LRW accuracy, 45.24% LRW-1000 accuracy, and 2.9% GRID WER / 1.2% CER under the stated dataset-specific conditions. See t3, t18, t32, t39, t48, and t72.

questions.q: What comparison or generalization claims should a reviewer qualify?
questions.answer: The authors claim state-of-the-art results and stronger cross-dataset transfer for face frontends, but give no multi-seed results; the aligned-face LRW result and hardest-pose Cutout result are caveats. See t4, t33–t34, t42, t52, t62, and t74.

questions.q: Which evaluation details are missing or limit reproducibility?
questions.answer: Seeds/repetitions, LRW speaker overlap, LRW-1000 test count, pixel normalization, checkpoint selection, GRID split seed/validation data, numeric chance baselines, and GRID beam/LM tuning parameters are not reported. See t74–t82.

questions.q: Which earlier works compared facial regions or used whole-face input, and what do the baselines in Tables III and VI come from?
questions.answer: Writer read the passages directly (Koumparoulis 2017, Vid2speech 2017, LCANet, LipNet, LRW-1000, Weng and Kitani 2019) and the later works (Zhang et al. 2022, Feng et al. 2020, SyncVSR 2024, Ma et al. 2022); entries c1-c29.
